defaults.permitted_development: Across Hampshire, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across Hampshire, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Hampshire, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: The wraparound fallback is narrow: both the side return and the rear projection have to satisfy Class A as one combined proposal. In Basingstoke and Deane, the wraparound has to stay balanced; once the side return and rear wing start to eat up the plot together, the design stops looking modest.

rules.height_rules: Single-storey wraparound elements still have to sit within the usual Class A height limits, with the side return often controlled by the 3m eaves rule near a boundary. In Basingstoke and Deane, roof discipline on the side arm usually does more to control bulk than squeezing extra depth out of the rear leg.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact on a wraparound is rarely just about depth; the side relationship and the rear-corner mass often create the real pressure point. In Basingstoke and Deane, what looks fine as separate measurements can still feel too heavy at the boundary once the wraparound is experienced as a single mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. On exposed coastal sites, roof profile, external finish and visual impact can carry more weight than on a routine suburban plot.
